title: The Meridian Library Audit: Reading Between the Lines
instructions: 这是一套原创的学术英语阅读练习（模拟材料，非官方雅思试题）。请先阅读三篇文章，然后完成40道题目。题目类型包括：单项选择、填空（答案必须来自原文，且不超过字数限制）、段落标题匹配（以单项选择形式呈现）以及判断题（True / False / Not Given）。判断题中，True表示原文明确支持；False表示原文明确矛盾；Not Given表示原文没有提供足够信息。所有解释均为中文，并附原文证据。建议限时完成：阅读+答题共75分钟。

PASSAGE 1

A. The Meridian Library, a mid-sized public institution in the town of Ashford, announced in January that it would conduct a full audit of its borrowing records. The decision followed a routine software update that revealed a persistent anomaly: for at least three years, the library’s automated system had been sending overdue notices to the wrong borrowers. According to the head librarian, Dr. Elena Marsh, the error affected roughly 12 per cent of all active accounts, though she stressed that no personal data had been lost or shared outside the library. “We are not dealing with a security breach,” she said at a press conference. “We are dealing with a bookkeeping failure that has caused unnecessary worry for hundreds of residents.”

B. The audit, which began on 3 February and is expected to last until the end of May, will examine every transaction recorded since 2019. A team of four librarians, assisted by two external auditors, will compare the digital logs with the physical borrowing cards that many older members still use. The library has also set up a dedicated telephone line for borrowers who believe they have received incorrect notices. Dr. Marsh admitted that the process would be slow. “We could simply wipe the records and start again,” she explained, “but that would erase the evidence we need to understand what went wrong. More importantly, it would be unfair to borrowers who have kept careful records of their own.”

C. Not everyone is satisfied with the library’s response. The Ashford Residents’ Association has collected more than 800 signatures on a petition demanding that the library waive all overdue fines incurred during the period affected by the error. The association’s chair, Mr. David Chen, argues that borrowers should not have to prove their innocence. “The library made the mistake,” he said. “Why should ordinary people spend hours on the phone trying to correct it?” Dr. Marsh has refused to cancel fines automatically, but she has promised that any borrower who can show a receipt or a bank statement proving that a fine was paid in error will receive a full refund. She has also agreed to extend the deadline for returning books by two weeks for anyone who received a faulty notice.

D. The audit has revealed some unexpected complications. Several borrowers whose accounts were flagged as overdue had in fact returned their books years earlier, but the returns had never been logged because the library’s scanning equipment was faulty. Others had borrowed books under a family member’s account, a practice the library had never formally prohibited but now discourages. In one case, a borrower had been receiving notices for a book that had been destroyed in a flood in 2021. “We found books that had been marked as lost for a decade,” said one auditor, who asked not to be named. “Some of them were sitting on the shelves the whole time.”

E. The financial impact of the error is difficult to calculate precisely. The library estimates that it has collected about £4,200 in fines that may have been issued incorrectly, but not all of that money will need to be refunded. Some borrowers, it turns out, genuinely returned their books late and simply ignored the notices. Others paid fines without checking whether they were correct. Dr. Marsh has ruled out a blanket refund, arguing that it would reward borrowers who had ignored their responsibilities. “We want to be fair, not generous,” she said. “Fairness means treating each case on its merits.”

F. The library has also taken steps to prevent a repeat of the problem. A new software system, scheduled to go live in June, will include an automatic cross-check that compares every overdue notice with the physical return records before it is sent. The library has allocated £18,000 for the upgrade, part of a larger technology budget approved by the town council in December. In addition, all staff will receive training on the new system, and the library will publish a monthly report on its website listing the number of notices sent and the number of errors identified. “Transparency is the best way to rebuild trust,” Dr. Marsh said.

G. The Residents’ Association remains sceptical. Mr. Chen has pointed out that the library has not yet agreed to an independent review of the audit’s findings. “They are marking their own homework,” he said. “How do we know the audit will be thorough?” Dr. Marsh has rejected this criticism, noting that two of the four auditors are external and that their report will be made public. She has also invited Mr. Chen to join a newly formed advisory committee that will oversee the implementation of the new system. At the time of writing, Mr. Chen had not yet responded to the invitation.

H. For many borrowers, the most frustrating aspect of the affair has been the uncertainty. Mrs. Patricia Hollis, a retired teacher who has used the library for over thirty years, received three overdue notices in January for books she had returned in November. “I telephoned the library four times,” she said. “Each time I was told someone would call me back, and nobody did.” She eventually visited the library in person and was able to resolve the issue in twenty minutes. “The staff were very apologetic,” she added. “But I shouldn’t have had to go there in person. I’m 78 years old.”

I. The library has acknowledged that its telephone response was inadequate. A spokesperson said that the volume of calls had overwhelmed the small team and that additional staff had now been assigned to the helpline. The library has also introduced a web form that allows borrowers to submit evidence of incorrect notices online, reducing the need for personal visits. Dr. Marsh has apologised publicly to Mrs. Hollis and to other borrowers who experienced similar difficulties. “We let people down,” she said. “We are determined to put it right.”

J. The audit is not expected to conclude until late May, and the full report will be published in June. In the meantime, the library has promised to keep borrowers informed through regular updates on its website and noticeboards. Whether these measures will satisfy the Residents’ Association remains to be seen. What is clear is that the affair has damaged the library’s reputation in a community that has always regarded it as a trusted institution. Rebuilding that trust, Dr. Marsh admits, will take more than a new software system. “It will take time,” she said. “But we are committed to getting it right.”

PASSAGE 2

A. In the small coastal town of Portwell, a group of residents has launched an ambitious project to restore the town’s historic salt marshes. The marshes, which once covered more than 400 hectares, have been reduced to less than 120 hectares over the past century, largely as a result of land reclamation for agriculture and housing. The Portwell Marsh Restoration Group, a volunteer organisation founded in 2022, aims to re-flood 60 hectares of former farmland and to reintroduce native plant species that have not been seen in the area for decades.

B. The project has not been without controversy. Local farmers have expressed concern that re-flooding the land could affect drainage on neighbouring fields and reduce the value of agricultural property. “We are not against conservation,” said Mr. Alan Pryce, who farms 80 hectares adjacent to the proposed site. “But we need to know that our livelihoods will not be damaged.” The restoration group has commissioned an independent hydrological study to assess the potential impact, and has promised to compensate any farmer who can demonstrate financial loss. The study is due to be completed in September.

C. Ecologists have welcomed the project, arguing that salt marshes provide valuable ecosystem services. According to Dr. Sarah Okonkwo, a marine biologist at the University of Westfield, salt marshes act as natural flood defences, absorbing wave energy and reducing coastal erosion. They also store carbon in their sediments, making them an important tool in the fight against climate change. “A healthy salt marsh can store more carbon per hectare than a tropical rainforest,” she said. “Restoring these habitats is one of the most cost-effective ways to address both flooding and climate change.”

D. The restoration group has raised £250,000 towards its £400,000 target. Most of the money has come from charitable trusts and private donations, with a smaller contribution from the town council. The group’s chair, Mrs. Helen Voss, said that the response from the local community had been encouraging. “We have received donations from over 600 individuals,” she said. “People understand that this is about protecting our town for future generations.”

E. The project is not the first of its kind in the region. A similar scheme in the neighbouring county of Northmoor, completed in 2018, successfully restored 45 hectares of marshland. According to a report published by the Northmoor Wildlife Trust, the scheme reduced flood risk for more than 200 homes and attracted a range of bird species that had not been seen in the area for years. However, the report also noted that the project had cost more than anticipated and that some farmers had experienced difficulties in obtaining compensation.

F. The Portwell group has learned from the Northmoor experience. It has established a compensation fund of £50,000 and has appointed a liaison officer to work directly with farmers. It has also committed to monitoring the site for at least ten years after restoration is complete. “We want to do this properly,” Mrs. Voss said. “That means listening to everyone, not just the people who agree with us.”

G. Not everyone is convinced. Some residents have questioned whether the project represents good value for money. “£400,000 is a lot of money for a piece of marshland,” said one local resident, who asked not to be named. “Couldn’t it be spent on something more useful, like a new health centre?” Mrs. Voss rejects this criticism, pointing out that the money has been raised specifically for the restoration project and could not be used for other purposes. “People are free to donate to whatever cause they choose,” she said. “But it is not either/or. We can have a health centre and a salt marsh.”

H. The restoration work is scheduled to begin in October, subject to the findings of the hydrological study. If all goes to plan, the first phase will involve breaching a sea wall to allow tidal water to flow onto the farmland. Native plants will then be introduced, and the site will be monitored by volunteers. The group hopes to see the return of species such as samphire and sea lavender within five years.

I. The project has also attracted interest from the local school. Pupils from Portwell Primary School have been involved in planting seeds in a nursery, and the group plans to install an educational boardwalk on the site. “It’s a living classroom,” said Mrs. Voss. “Children who grow up with the marsh will understand why it matters.”

J. The long-term success of the project will depend on many factors, including the findings of the hydrological study, the availability of funding, and the willingness of farmers to cooperate. But for now, the group remains optimistic. “We are at the beginning of a long journey,” Mrs. Voss said. “But we are determined to see it through.”

PASSAGE 3

A. The relationship between sleep and academic performance has been the subject of considerable research in recent years. While it is widely accepted that sleep is important for learning, the precise mechanisms remain a matter of debate. A new study conducted by researchers at the University of Ashford has added to the evidence, suggesting that the timing of sleep may be as important as its duration.

B. The study, which followed 1,200 university students over a two-year period, found that students who went to bed and woke up at consistent times performed better on tests of memory and attention than those whose sleep schedules varied by more than two hours from day to day. The difference was modest but statistically significant: on average, consistent sleepers scored 6 per cent higher on the tests. “We are not talking about a magic bullet,” said Dr. James Whitfield, the study’s lead author. “But the findings suggest that regularity matters.”

C. The study has been criticised by some researchers for relying on self-reported sleep data. Participants were asked to keep sleep diaries and to complete questionnaires, rather than having their sleep monitored objectively. “Self-reported data can be unreliable,” said Professor Linda Marsh of the University of Northfield. “People tend to overestimate how much they sleep and underestimate how much their schedules vary.” Dr. Whitfield acknowledges this limitation but points out that the study also used data from wearable devices for a subset of 300 participants, and that the results were consistent with the self-reported data.

D. The findings are consistent with a growing body of evidence linking sleep regularity to health outcomes. A separate study, published last year, found that irregular sleep patterns were associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, even among people who slept for seven to eight hours a night on average. Another study suggested that shift workers, whose sleep schedules are by definition irregular, are more likely to experience cognitive decline in later life.

E. However, the relationship between sleep and academic performance is complex. A student who sleeps regularly but for only five hours a night is unlikely to perform well, regardless of consistency. Conversely, a student who sleeps for nine hours but at different times each day may still perform adequately. “Duration and regularity are both important,” Dr. Whitfield said. “Neither should be ignored.”

F. The study also found that the timing of sleep mattered. Students who went to bed after 2 a.m. performed worse than those who went to bed before midnight, even when the total duration of sleep was the same. This finding is consistent with research on circadian rhythms, which suggests that the body’s internal clock is optimised for sleep during the hours of darkness. “Staying up late and sleeping in may not fully compensate for the loss of sleep at the right time,” Dr. Whitfield explained.

G. Not all researchers agree that the findings have practical implications. “Students cannot always control their schedules,” said Professor Marsh. “They have deadlines, part-time jobs, and social commitments. Telling them to go to bed at the same time every night is not necessarily helpful.” Dr. Whitfield accepts this point but argues that small changes can make a difference. “We are not suggesting that students should never stay up late,” he said. “But they should be aware that regular sleep is likely to benefit their studies.”

H. The study’s authors have called for further research, particularly studies that use objective measures of sleep over longer periods. They also suggest that universities could play a role in promoting healthy sleep habits, for example by scheduling classes later in the morning and by providing information about sleep hygiene. “Universities have a responsibility to create an environment that supports learning,” Dr. Whitfield said. “That includes thinking about how schedules affect sleep.”

I. The findings are unlikely to surprise anyone who has struggled to concentrate after a poor night’s sleep. But they add to a growing body of evidence that sleep is not simply a passive state but an active process that is essential for learning and memory. As Dr. Whitfield put it: “Sleep is not a luxury. It is a fundamental part of how we learn.”

J. The study is due to be published in full later this year. In the meantime, the authors have made their data available to other researchers, a decision that has been welcomed by the scientific community. “Open data is essential for progress,” said Professor Marsh, who, despite her criticisms, praised the authors for their transparency. “We may disagree about the interpretation, but we can all agree that the data should be shared.”

SECTION 1: SOCIAL DIALOGUE

Man: Hello, is this the Meridian Library helpline?
Woman: Yes, it is. How can I help you?
Man: Hi, my name’s Tom Bradley. I received an overdue notice for a book I’m sure I returned. It’s called The Lost Gardens.
Woman: Let me check. Can you give me your library card number, please?
Man: Yes, it’s 4-7-2-9-1-0-3.
Woman: Thank you. I’m seeing a notice was sent on the 14th of January. Do you remember when you returned the book?
Man: I think it was the 3rd of January. I definitely returned it before the 10th, because that’s when I went on holiday.
Woman: Okay. Sometimes the scanning machine misses a return. I’ll mark it as returned and cancel the fine. You won’t need to pay anything.
Man: That’s great, thank you. Will I get a confirmation?
Woman: Yes, we’ll send you an email within 24 hours. Is the email address on your account still correct?
Man: It should be. It’s tom.bradley at email dot com.
Woman: Got it. And just to let you know, we’re extending the return deadline by two weeks for anyone who received a faulty notice.
Man: Oh, right. So I can keep my other books a bit longer?
Woman: Exactly. Until the 28th of February.
Man: Perfect. Thanks for your help.
Woman: You’re welcome. Have a good day.

SECTION 2: SOCIAL MONOLOGUE

Good morning, everyone. This is Helen Voss from the Portwell Marsh Restoration Group with a quick update. First, I’m delighted to announce that we have now raised £250,000 towards our £400,000 target. That’s thanks to over 600 individual donors, as well as a generous contribution from the town council. Second, the hydrological study is now underway and should be completed by September. We know that some farmers are worried about drainage, and we want to reassure them that we will compensate anyone who can demonstrate financial loss. Third, we are planning a public meeting on the 15th of March at the community centre. Everyone is welcome, whether you support the project or not. Fourth, I want to remind you that the restoration work is scheduled to begin in October, subject to the findings of the study. Finally, I’d like to thank the pupils from Portwell Primary School, who have been helping us plant seeds in the nursery. It’s wonderful to see young people getting involved. If you have any questions, please email us or come along to the meeting. Thank you.

SECTION 3: ACADEMIC DISCUSSION

Tutor: So, James, you’ve been looking at the sleep study. What did you make of it?
Student: Well, I thought the findings were interesting, but I wasn’t convinced by the methodology. They relied on self-reported data, didn’t they?
Tutor: That’s right. But they did use wearable devices for a subset of participants. Does that address your concern?
Student: Partly. But 300 out of 1,200 is only a quarter. And the wearable data was only collected for a short period, I think.
Tutor: Yes, that’s a fair point. What about the finding that consistent sleepers scored 6 per cent higher? Is that meaningful?
Student: It’s statistically significant, but is it practically significant? A 6 per cent difference might not matter much in the real world.
Tutor: That’s a good question. Dr. Whitfield himself said it wasn’t a magic bullet. But he argued that small effects can add up over time.
Student: I suppose. But I also wondered about the sample. They were all university students, so can we generalise to other populations?
Tutor: We can’t, strictly speaking. That’s a limitation. But the study does add to a growing body of evidence. Did you notice the point about timing?
Student: Yes, going to bed after 2 a.m. was associated with worse performance, even when duration was the same. That seems consistent with circadian rhythm research.
Tutor: Exactly. And that’s perhaps the most practical finding. It suggests that when you sleep matters, not just how long.
Student: But as Professor Marsh pointed out, students can’t always control their schedules.
Tutor: True. But the authors argue that small changes can help. And they suggest universities could schedule classes later.
Student: That would be popular with students, I imagine.
Tutor: Indeed. Okay, let’s move on to the next study.

SECTION 4: ACADEMIC LECTURE

Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about the concept of ecosystem services, using salt marshes as a case study. Salt marshes are coastal wetlands that are flooded and drained by tides. They are found in many parts of the world, but they have been declining rapidly. In the UK, for example, more than 80 per cent of salt marshes have been lost over the past two centuries, mainly due to land reclamation.

So why should we care? Salt marshes provide a range of ecosystem services. First, they act as natural flood defences. The dense vegetation slows down water flow and absorbs wave energy, reducing the risk of flooding for coastal communities. Second, they store carbon. The sediments in salt marshes are anaerobic, which means they lack oxygen, and this slows down decomposition. As a result, carbon accumulates over time. A healthy salt marsh can store more carbon per hectare than a tropical rainforest. Third, they provide habitat for wildlife. Many bird species, fish, and invertebrates depend on salt marshes for breeding, feeding, and shelter.

Despite these benefits, salt marshes continue to be lost. The main threats are coastal development, pollution, and sea-level rise. Restoration projects, like the one in Portwell, aim to reverse this decline. But restoration is not without challenges. It can be expensive, and it can conflict with other land uses, such as agriculture. That’s why projects need to engage with local communities and address their concerns.

In conclusion, salt marshes are valuable ecosystems that provide essential services. Protecting and restoring them is not just an environmental issue; it is also an economic and social one. Thank you. I’m happy to take questions.

grammar.title: 否定、比较、数量范围和时态；限定词的含义
grammar.explanation: 本单元重点复习否定结构（如 not necessarily, unlikely to）、比较结构（如 more than, less than, as important as）、数量范围（如 roughly, at least, more than）以及时态（如现在完成时、过去时）和限定词（如 all, some, any, no）的准确含义。这些语法点在阅读理解中常影响对事实范围的判断。
grammar.example: The error affected roughly 12 per cent of all active accounts.
